issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise' is not clinically coherent with the rest of the profile. The threat items center on hypervigilance about nighttime intrusion and safety checking in the home, while the memory and appraisal items focus on intrusive assault memories, danger, and physical vulnerability. Exercise avoidance addresses a different symptom domain and lacks plausible linkage to the selected threat, memory, or appraisal content. In contrast, magical thinking and mirror checking fit better with maladaptive attempts to manage threat and distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: These two selected items are difficult to reconcile within the same profile. A strong appraisal of permanent bodily damage implies acknowledgment of serious ongoing physical consequences, whereas telling oneself the event did not really happen or was not that bad reflects minimization/denial of the trauma's reality or impact. While some ambivalence can occur clinically, this pair pulls in opposing directions strongly enough to question internal coherence in this profile.

vignette:
Mariama was seventy-eight years old, a potter whose hands had known the rhythm of clay for over fifty years. She had been born in a small village in West Africa and had come to America in her thirties, building a life, a family, a home. Her husband, Kwame, had died twelve years ago, and she had learned to live with the quiet of the house. She had never been afraid of the silence. Now, she was afraid of everything.

The assault had happened in her own studio, the small converted garage behind her house where she kept her wheel and kiln. It was late afternoon, and she had been alone, cleaning up after a long day. She heard the back gate creak and assumed it was the wind. Then the door to the studio swung open, and a man was there — young, desperate, his eyes scanning the room before they landed on her. He demanded money. She had none. He became enraged. He shoved her hard against the wall, and she fell, her hip striking the concrete floor. He grabbed her purse, which held only a few dollars and her bus pass, and then he was gone. The entire event lasted less than two minutes. But for Mariama, those two minutes never ended.

The memory did not behave like other memories. It arrived without warning, a sudden, unbidden image of the man’s face, the angle of his shoulder as he pushed her, the cold shock of the floor. She would be sitting at her kitchen table, a cup of tea in her hands, and then she was back in the studio, feeling the impact, hearing her own gasp, her heart lurching as if the threat were still immediate. The memories were almost entirely visual — pictures that flashed behind her eyes, sharp and vivid, and each time they came she felt the same terror, the same helplessness, as if she were reliving it all over again. She had come to believe that if she let herself think about the event in any deliberate way, she would not be able to handle it. The feelings would overwhelm her, swallow her whole. So she tried, with all her strength, to push the thoughts away. She would shake her head, stand up abruptly, turn on the television to drown out her own mind. But the images came anyway, slipping past her defenses like water through cracked clay.

Her home, which had always been her sanctuary, had become a place of constant vigilance. She could not relax. Even when she knew, logically, that she was safe — the doors locked, the neighborhood quiet, the afternoon sun streaming through her window — her body remained tense, braced for something. She would catch herself listening, straining to hear sounds that might mean someone was entering. The creak of a floorboard. The distant hum of a car slowing down. At night, she woke repeatedly, her eyes snapping open in the dark, her breath shallow, her first thought a single, urgent question: Am I safe? She would lie still, listening, before she allowed herself to move. She had developed a ritual of checking the locks on every door and window, sometimes three or four times before she could settle into bed. She knew it was excessive. She could not stop.

The mirror checking had started a few weeks after the assault. She did not fully understand why she did it, only that she felt compelled. She would glance at her reflection in the bathroom mirror, then look again a moment later, as if needing to confirm that she was still herself, that the face looking back at her had not been changed by what had happened. She checked in the hallway mirror, in the small mirror she kept by the back door. Each time, she felt a flicker of relief that she looked the same, followed by a deeper unease that she was not the same at all. Her body, she had come to feel, had betrayed her. It kept reacting as if she were still in danger, flooding her with adrenaline when there was nothing to run from, keeping her alert and trembling in a house that held no threat. She felt estranged from her own skin.

The world, Mariama now believed, was a dangerous place. This was not an abstract idea; it was a conviction that colored every decision. She had stopped working in her studio. The wheel sat untouched, the clay drying out on the shelf. She could not bring herself to go back there, even during the day. She had always sold her pots at a local craft market, but she had stopped attending. The thought of being in a crowd, of not being able to see who was behind her, made her chest tighten. A neighbor had offered to drive her to the grocery store, but she had declined, preferring to order what she needed online. Her daughter called every evening, and Mariama would tell her she was fine, that she was just tired, that she did not need anything. What she needed was to feel that the fear would end. She had come to a point where she could no longer bear the weight of it alone, and that was what finally brought her to seek help. She was afraid of what her life had become — a narrow room of rituals and dread — and she was desperate to find her way back to the woman who had shaped clay with her hands and not been afraid of the silence.
